1:
Who wrote the psalm is disputed before a word of it is read. John Calvin notes that David’s name is not in the inscription and that many conjecture the sons of Korah for its authors, which he thinks not at all probable: it is composed in the person of David, who was endued above all others with the spirit of prophecy and had already delivered other psalms to the Levites to sing. They are named, he concludes, because the psalm was committed to them. Adam Clarke takes the other side: such psalms were probably composed by the descendants of Korah during the Babylonish captivity, or by some eminent person among them, and used through it as means of consolation. He records what the versions made of it — the Syriac calling it a psalm David sang in exile, desiring to return; the Arabic a psalm for the backsliding Jews. Keil and Delitzsch take the naming of a family rather than a man as the striking thing, comparing the way a German hymn-book will credit a brotherhood instead of an author; they also open the book with a count, the first book using one divine name two hundred and seventy-two times against fifteen while this second reverses the proportion.

Why the hart pants is the next question. John Gill canvasses the possibilities: a natural thirst, the heat of summer, or the hunt, when the creature takes to the rivers partly to escape and partly to extinguish its thirst. Since the verb is feminine, he adds, the Septuagint made it a hind, Kimchi supposing the female’s voice the stronger though the philosopher says the reverse. Adam Clarke settles on the chase, citing Tuberville that a hart nearly spent takes to a river and keeps in it as long as his breath will let him. C.H. Spurgeon allows both pictures — the fainting hind after a drought, or rather the hunted hart seeking the river to lave its smoking flanks and escape the dogs — and turns the sound of it into an epigram, that as the hart brays so his soul prays. Debarred from public worship, David sought neither ease nor honour but communion, not as a luxury but as a necessity, like water to a stag. Charles Ellicott supplies an eyewitness instead of an argument, quoting a traveller who saw flocks of panting harts gather round the water-brooks in the deserts of Syria, so subdued by thirst that one could approach quite near before they fled.

What the longing is for divides the last comments. Augustine of Hippo makes the speaker corporate: who is it that says this? It is ourselves, if we be but willing — not one individual but one Body, since Christ’s Body is the Church. He then records a use rather than a meaning: it is not ill understood of catechumens hastening to the grace of the holy Font, on which account it is ordinarily chanted then, though he holds the longing is not fully satisfied even in the faithful at their Baptism. Matthew Henry makes the desire itself the test, holy love being the life and soul of religion without which all external professions are but a shell and carcase; God teaches us the worth of mercies by the want of them, and lamenting after him is as sure an evidence that we love him as rejoicing in him. Charles Ellicott observes that the metaphor is worth notice only because God himself is here the object of the thirst, where elsewhere it is righteousness or knowledge. Adam Clarke puts the words in a Christian mouth — when shall I see my heavenly country? — and adds that a man who feels himself here at home, whose soul is not spiritual, feels no panting after the living God. John Gill and John Wesley set the living God against the idols, which are lifeless statues.
3:
Tears for food is read literally by everyone. John Gill says simply that he could not eat for sorrow, like Hannah. Adam Clarke divides the cause: the longing after spiritual blessings was so intense that he forgot to take his necessary food, and the sorrow so great that he had no appetite for any — and he feels more for the honour of God and his truth than for himself when the idolaters who hold the people in captivity insultingly cry, Where is thy God? Charles Ellicott adds a classical parallel, a line of Ovid in which care and grief of mind and tears were a man’s nourishment.

The remembering is where the entry becomes difficult. John Gill offers a choice, either the reproaches of the enemies or rather the past enjoyments of God in his house. Adam Clarke takes the second and lets it run: these things often occur to me and sharpen my distressful feelings, and my soul is dissolved, becomes weak as water, when I reflect on what I have had and lost. There was a multitude to worship God in public, and with these I often went; now there are only a few solitary individuals who sigh for the desolations of Zion, and no processions, no festivals, no joyous assemblies. Then he stops and says why: he has given a general sense, but there are several difficulties in the verse, and commentators and critics have given it a great variety of translations and as many meanings, which his plan will not permit him to follow — the reader is sent to Horsley instead. Charles Ellicott names the trouble Clarke declines to enter. The conjunction when is not expressed but may be implied from the next clause; the phrase rendered I pour out my soul in me may mean that the poet weeps floods of tears over his own lot; and the versions, together with the strangeness of the words rendered multitude and went with them, indicate a corruption of the text, though the general sense of the verse is independent of the doubtful expressions. The festival recalled, he thinks, is probably the Feast of Tabernacles, and the word rendered kept holyday means literally dancing or reeling, dancing having been a recognised part of the ceremonial. John Wesley keeps to the plain reading: the remembering is of his banishment and his enemies’ triumphs, the pouring out is of sorrows breathed within his own breast, the multitudes are Israelites who went up in great numbers, and the holy day is the three solemn festivals kept to the Lord.

The refrain then interrupts, and what it is doing is described two ways. John Gill takes it as self-correction, the psalmist expostulating with himself for being too much depressed by his present circumstances. Adam Clarke supplies the argument: bad as the times are, desolate as Jerusalem is, hopeless as the condition may look in the sight of man, there is no room for despair, since all things are possible to God and there is a promise of restoration. Charles Ellicott hears it differently, as a sigh breaking in on the song, the spirit of dejection struggling against the spirit of faith. He also wants the words themselves corrected: cast down is better rendered bowed down, and in the original with a middle sense, why bowest thou down thyself; disquieted comes from a root kindred to our word hum; and there is no question, he says, that the refrain must be read here exactly as it stands at its later occurrences, since the versions already do so, one Hebrew manuscript notices the wrong accentuation, and without the change the rhythm is defective. John Wesley glosses the last clause from the Hebrew as the salvations of his face, meaning the supports and deliverances he does not doubt he will enjoy both in God’s presence and from the light of his countenance.
6:
The second dejection is quieter than the first, and two voices say why. Matthew Henry observes that complaints and comforts here take their turn like day and night, and finds the support in the access itself: when we cannot get relief by pleading with ourselves, we should try praying to God and leaving our case with him, for we cannot still these winds and waves, but we know who can. The way to forget the sense of our miseries, he adds, is to remember the God of our mercies. C.H. Spurgeon hears the psalm start over: the song begins again upon the brass, the spasm of despondency having returned, and the singer takes down his harp to try its power on himself as he had seen it work on Saul. But he is more tranquil now, the outward expression of desire gone and the sorrow restrained within doors. John Gill notes that the repetition shows the greatness of the dejection without loss of interest in God, and introduces the remedy, a calling to mind of past experiences of divine goodness.

Where he is when he says it divides the entry. Adam Clarke takes the land of Jordan for Judea, explains the plural Hermons by the mountain’s double ridge rising in many summits, and reports Bishop Horsley’s view that the little hill is Zion, little in comparison of the Hermons. Charles Ellicott puts the poet further out and refuses the identification. The land of Jordan is the uplands of the north-east where the river rises; the poet has not yet passed quite into exile but is on its borders, and as his sad eyes turn back towards the country he is leaving, its sacred summits disappear while nearer and higher rise the snow-clad peaks of Hermon. The plural is either collective for the range or refers to a ridge with a peak at either end. As for the little hill, it cannot well be Zion, since the custom of Hebrew poetry was to exalt Zion and not to depreciate the higher mountains; some lower hill near at hand is the natural supposition. John Wesley declines to place it at all, taking the names for all the parts of the land to which he should be driven, east of Jordan or north at Hermon.

The noise of the waterspouts is explained by meteorology, by geography and by metaphor. Adam Clarke gives the physics: a waterspout is a large tube formed of clouds by means of the electric fluid, the base uppermost and the point let down perpendicularly, which attracts vast quantities of water and pours it down in torrents; such spouts are frequent on the coast of Syria, and Dr. Shaw saw them at Mount Carmel. He also hears the Hebrew itself as sound-painting, one wave rolling on impelled by another. Charles Ellicott prefers flood calling unto flood at the noise of thy cataracts, since the exile is describing what was before his eyes: the windings and rapids of the Jordan, each hurrying to dash itself over some opposing ledge in cataract after cataract to the sea, so that every step of that journey offered an emblem of his accumulating griefs. The waves and billows are by derivation breakers and rollers, and the poet forgets the source of his image in its intensity, passing on to a sea of troubles. John Gill and John Wesley keep it figurative, the one taking the deeps for afflictions arriving one after another as in the case of Job, the other for violent and successive showers coming down as at the call of God. On the promise that follows, John Gill reads the daytime as a fit and seasonable time, or openly, or continually, while Charles Ellicott prefers by day the Lord shall command his grace, and thinks the parallelism confirms that the words prayer and song were used indiscriminately of any hymn in religious use.
9:
The complaint and the reproach run together here, and Adam Clarke thinks the English has joined them wrongly. This verse and the next, he says, are badly pointed in our Bibles, and he repunctuates so that the sword belongs to the mourning rather than to the reproach: why go I mourning as with a sword in my bones because of the oppression of the enemy? Mine enemies reproach me daily, while they say unto me, Where is thy God? The reproaches, on his reading, are as cutting and severe as a sword thrust into the body and separating between the bones — and this because they are aimed past the sufferer at God himself, as if he had not power to save his people out of the hands of their oppressors. John Gill finds the trouble in the manuscripts rather than the punctuation, noting a various reading in which some copies have in, or with, and others as, the last of which seems to him the truest, while the translators have supplied as to make the sense although they read with. John Wesley takes the received sense without comment, a sword which cutteth the very bones, so painful are their reproaches. Charles Ellicott adds only that we apparently have here the very words of the prayer mentioned just before. John Gill notes that the name my rock is one frequently given to the eternal God.

On the refrain Adam Clarke repeats his argument against despair, that God will appear and release the captives and their sighing shall soon flee away, and explains the health of the countenance from the body: as a healthy constitution shows itself in the appearance of the face, so God will heal the spiritual maladies and the face will testify the happiness within. John Gill observes only that the expostulation is the same as before.

Then Adam Clarke closes the chapter with something he says he cannot withhold from the reader, a curious gloss on the first verse from his old Psalter. It renders the opening in its own English — as the hart yearns for the wells of waters, so my soul yearns to God — and paraphrases that this psalm is all of perfect men, who are burning in the flame of God’s love and pass into the contemplative life, and that it is therefore sung in the office of the dead, since they have then what they yearned for, which is the sight of God. The gloss goes on: as the hart that has eaten the adder greatly yearns to come to the wells of water, to drink and grow young again, so, vices and uncleanness being destroyed in me, my soul desires with burning yearning to come to God. Adam Clarke then supplies the natural history behind it, that Aelian, Nicander, Pliny and other ancient writers all report that the hart thirsts because it eats serpents, whose poison diffused through its entrails produces a burning heat and fever which it cures with water; many of the fathers tell the same tale, and it is from them, he says, that the paraphrast borrowed.
